newsitem.title: UK: Owen quits NatWest Markets as focus shifts.
newsitem.headline: Owen quits NatWest Markets as focus shifts.

text.p: British banking giant NatWest on Monday issued a profit warning and promptly announced a strategy rethink at its investment banking unit NatWest Markets which included the exit of chief executive Martin Owen.
NatWest said in a statement Owen had resigned with immediate effect and would be replaced by NatWest chief Derek Wanless until a replacement could be found.
Shares in the bank dropped to 776-1/2 pence right after the announcement, retreating from a high of 821 pence. By 1429 GMT, the shares fell even further to 757 1/2 pence.
Owen's future has been under question since late February when NatWest Markets disclosed it had sustained multi-million pound losses in its derivatives division over a sustained period.
His departure coincides with a major shift in focus by NatWest Markets, which had aimed to be one of the top ten global investment banking firms.
"What surprises me is that 12 or 18 months after they started pumping money into this area they should seem to be having second thoughts," one dealer said.
The bank did not say why Owen was leaving but paid tribute to his "considerable contribution".
At the time Owen said he would forego 200,000 pounds of a 500,000 pound bonus although Wanless said he still had confidence in him. Owen has been head of the investment bank since 1992.

The change in direction is also a response to shareholder demands for better performance from NatWest, which has lagged rivals such as Lloyds TSB Group Plc, which has concentrated on retail banking and steamed ahead of its competitors.
NatWest did not say it would retreat entirely from investment banking but would instead refocus its efforts within the division.
"Our focus will be on areas where we have a competitive advantage with a strong product or research base and high quality people," NatWest's Wanless said.
This would mean "deploying capital in those investment banking activities where better returns can be achieved," he added.

The group also disclosed the full impact of the interest rate options losses uncovered in February by warning profits for the whole group for the first half of the year would not exceed 770 million pounds ($1.3 billion).
"This incident has had a knock-on effect on the profits at NatWest Markets," NatWest said.
Banking analysts had expected a considerably better figure for the six months to the end of June, with one forecasting pre-tax profits in the region of 900 million pounds before the warning.
NatWest made it clear the revision was entirely due to the problems at NatWest Markets.

"Profits for the first half of 1997 at NatWest Markets, excluding the 77 million pound net charge against pre-tax profits related to the interest rate options mispricing, are expected to be significantly lower than for the same period last year," it said.
But the continuing businesses of the group were expected to show an improved performance in the first half of the year compared with 1996.
The bank is due to report its results for the first half of the year in August.

NatWest said an independent probe into what went wrong in its interest rate options business was nearing completion, adding an announcement on the report's main findings would be made by the end of June. This was originally due by the end of May.

The report, by City accountants Coopers & Lybrand and law firm Linklaters & Paines, has already been passed to the Bank of England and financial markets watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), bankers said.
It is not yet clear what action, if any, the regulators will take against NatWest Markets or any of the individuals responsible for the division where the interest rate option losses occurred.
A total of five managers have been suspended as a result of the losses and millions of pounds in bonuses were clawed back after the problems came to light. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
